leads.name: Bland Oak
leads.status: RESOLVED 2026-09-05, delivered as syd_007 (data/research/_famous-australia-verified.json), container: sydney (existing city). Verified alive and actively maintained (2020 acorn-propagation programme, ongoing council National Tree Day recognition). Species corrected from the genus guess to Southern Live Oak (Quercus virginiana) per Wikipedia's infobox (a WebSearch summary wrongly called it Quercus robur; the directly-fetched page was trusted instead). Planted 1842 by William Bland, documented planting date, so age ~184 years rather than an estimate. Two sources: Wikipedia and Fairfield City Council's own Heritage Collection. Public council park, no access restriction, reachable by Carramar station (Sydney Trains T5 Cumberland Line).

leads.name: Centurion tree
leads.status: RESOLVED 2026-09-05, delivered as hob_011 (data/research/_famous-australia-verified.json), container: hobart (existing city, 11th entry, proposed as a day-trip-by-car addition). Verified alive as of a Jan 2025 Guardian report (96m tall after 2019 bushfire damage, down from a 2018 laser-measured peak of 100.5m). Species Eucalyptus regnans, no documented age. Two sources: Wikipedia and ABC News (2018). Coordinates confirmed from Wikipedia's infobox (tree-level, LiDAR-identified). Access is free/no permission needed via forestry road and a self-guided walking track, but genuinely remote: no public transport, 1.5-2 hour drive south of Hobart, no phone coverage.

leads.name: Gregory's Tree
leads.status: RESOLVED 2026-09-05, delivered as gtr_001 (data/research/_famous-australia-verified.json), container: new place: Gregory's Tree / Timber Creek, NT. Verified alive per the NT Heritage Register's own site page (Place ID 101, calls it 'a living monument'), boab (Adansonia gregorii), tree-level coordinates from the register's site map. Public heritage reserve on the Victoria Highway with a boardwalk and interpretative panels; also a registered Aboriginal sacred site (Ngaringman people), which restricts touching the trunk but not viewing. NOTE: the Commons photos' 'Roper River' caption looks like an archive mislabelling; the actual documented tree is near Timber Creek, ~500km from the Roper.
leads.note: geographically the 'Roper River' filename/caption on these Commons photos does not match the actual Timber Creek site; do not use it to place a pin if these photos are picked up in a later photo pass

leads.name: Hoop Pines, Bald Hills
leads.species_basis: confirmed by Queensland Heritage Register listing and Wikipedia
leads.age_estimate: taller tree ~190 years, smaller ~140 years (per Queensland Heritage Register citation)
leads.note: A genuinely compact pair, one site, historically significant (marks the original Stewart Farmhouse site, among the earliest non-Indigenous settlement in Bald Hills; hoop pine logging was one reason for the Moreton Bay penal settlement). BLOCKED ON ACCESS ONLY, not on quality: the pair stands 'at the end of the school's main driveway, framing the entrance to the Administration Building' of St Paul's Anglican School, a 51-hectare private campus at 34 Strathpine Road; no source found stating the driveway or entrance is open to the public without a school reason to be there. Per the school-grounds rule this stays a lead rather than a block: if a future pass finds evidence of genuine public access (a public path, visibility from Strathpine Road itself, stated open days) it can ship. Not researched further in this pass (checked 2026-09-01).

leads.name: Leichhardt Tree, Comet
leads.reason: CONFIRMED DEAD, never publish as a collectible entry. This coolabah tree at the confluence of the Comet and Nogoa Rivers was scarfed by Ludwig Leichhardt's expedition on 5 March 1847 (marked 'DIG L' with an arrow over a buried canister of letters), but the tree itself was felled in the 1950s out of fear it would be lost to fire; the marked trunk section was removed to Brisbane, displayed for years at Newstead House, and now sits in storage/museum display (offered to the Royal Historical Society of Queensland for the Miles Historical Village Museum). Only a 1975 memorial plaque marks the original site today, not a living tree (checked 2026-09-05, multiple tourism/history sources corroborate the felling and relocation of the trunk). This is a DIFFERENT tree from the separately heritage-listed 'Leichhardt Tree, Taroom' (Queensland Heritage Register #600835, marked 1844), which was not part of this pass's remit and was not checked.

leads.name: Pillar Box, Claremont
leads.reason: the tree itself is GONE, not a collectible living tree. Heritage Council of WA's own inHerit register (Place #00495, 256 Stirling Hwy Claremont) lists this heritage item as the 'Pillar Box', officially 'Site of the Halfway Tree': a tall tuart tree that was the mail-exchange meeting point for Perth and Fremantle postmen until 1863, later a fashionable afternoon-drive destination, but the tree was severely lopped in the early 20th century and only a stump remained by 1935. What survives and is heritage-listed today is an 1868 cast-iron pillar postbox marking the historic site, a structure rather than a tree (checked 2026-09-05, source: inherit.dplh.wa.gov.au Place 00495).

leads.name: The Old Gum Tree
leads.species_basis: genus read from the tree's own name; ask the reader which species
leads.reason: CONFIRMED DEAD, never publish as a collectible entry. This is the tree at Glenelg North, South Australia under which Governor John Hindmarsh read the proclamation founding the colony of South Australia on 28 December 1836. The original tree died long ago; its decayed husk was encased in concrete in 1963 to preserve its shape, and it now stands as a preserved monument/relic under a shelter with a plaque, not a living tree (checked 2026-09-05, sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Old_Gum_Tree, abc.net.au/news/2017-12-28/why-is-a-concrete-filled-bent-old-gum-tree-significant-in-sa/9289356). It remains an active annual Proclamation Day ceremony site but fails the never-dead-as-a-collectible-entry rule regardless of its ongoing civic significance.

leads.name: Tree of Knowledge (Australia)
leads.reason: CONFIRMED DEAD, never publish as a collectible entry. This ~200-year-old ghost gum (Corymbia aparrerinja) outside Barcaldine railway station, Oak Street, Barcaldine, Queensland (site of the 1891 Shearers' Strike meetings and the 1892 reading of the manifesto that founded the Australian Labor Party; Queensland Heritage Register #600021) was poisoned with glyphosate in May 2006, declared dead by an arborist on 3 October 2006, and its remains removed 29 July 2007. The preserved dead trunk now stands inside a purpose-built sculptural memorial pergola (opened 2 May 2009, won a national heritage architecture award), a monument rather than a living tree (checked 2026-09-05, source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_of_Knowledge_(Australia)). NOTE FOR A FUTURE PASS: several cuttings taken before its death were propagated; the tree was cloned in 2008 by the former Queensland DPI, with clones reportedly growing in Barcaldine itself, one planted at the Ecosciences Precinct in Brisbane, and one planted by PM Julia Gillard at the National Arboretum Canberra in 2011. None of these is documented as a single, publicly designated 'the' Tree of Knowledge replacement at a specific point in Barcaldine (unlike the Elm of Saint-Gervais precedent), so per hard rule this stays blocked rather than being redirected to a clone; a future pass could check whether Barcaldine's own cuttings have since been consolidated into one named, signposted specimen.

blocked.name: Kelvin Grove Fig Trees and Air Raid Shelter
blocked.species_basis: genus read from the tree's own name; ask the reader which species
blocked.reason: not a collectible point: the Queensland Heritage listing covers three separate fig groupings (5 trees at Normanby Fiveways, 7 at Marshall Park, 3 at Prospect Terrace) strung along a full kilometre of Kelvin Grove Road, with no single obvious place to stand, the same 'avenue' shape as the rejected Plane Trees of La Rambla precedent (checked 2026-09-01, source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin_Grove_Fig_Trees_and_Air_Raid_Shelter). If wanted later, the Prospect Terrace corner alone (3 weeping figs plus the WWII air raid shelter, now a bus shelter, with a fig branch grown onto its roof) is a narrower, genuinely compact candidate that was not separately researched in this pass.

blocked.name: Separation Tree
blocked.reason: CONFIRMED DEAD, never publish as a collectible entry. This 400-year-old river red gum (Eucalyptus camaldulensis) on Tennyson Lawn, Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria, was ringbarked by vandals in 2010 (about 90% of cambial tissue removed) and again in 2013 (the remaining 10% destroyed); Melbourne Gardens' own director confirmed it dead, and the canopy plus parts of the trunk were lopped in 2015 for safety, leaving only the main trunk and three scaffold limbs standing by July 2015 as a monument, not a living tree (checked 2026-09-03, sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_Tree, abc.net.au/news/2015-01-06/separation-tree-in-melbournes-botanic-gardens-unlikely-to-survive/6001782, gardendrum.com/2015/03/02/historic-separation-tree-lost-forever). NOTE FOR A FUTURE PASS: 26 saplings propagated from the original's seed have been planted around Victoria, including one back in the Royal Botanic Gardens itself and one at Parliament House Gardens (per Wikipedia, citing Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria sources); per CLAUDE.md's rule that a fallen original honestly succeeded by a living replanting may pass when the entry describes the LIVING tree, one of these specific saplings could in principle become a Melbourne entry, but none was individually located, aged or verified in this pass, so this remains a lead rather than a publishable tree.

blocked.name: Kidman's Tree of Knowledge
blocked.reason: Coolibah (Eucalyptus coolibah) at Glengyle Station, Bedourie, Shire of Diamantina, Queensland, ~60km south of Bedourie on the western bank of Eyre Creek. Reputedly where Sir Sidney Kidman camped while contemplating his pastoral empire (Wikipedia itself calls the connection unproven). Queensland Heritage Register #600462, listed 1992. Described as healthy and mature, standing in a grassed square formed by the homestead and its outbuildings. BLOCKED: sits inside the working homestead compound of Glengyle Station, a private pastoral property still run by S Kidman and Company; no evidence of any public access, visitor path or invitation. Fails hard rule 10 (private working station, not genuinely open to visitors) and fails the single-tree-destination test as a result: nobody can simply travel there, it is deep in a remote station's home paddock 60km from the nearest town. Not a case of inconvenience (a gate that might be shut) but of no public access existing at all.
